source_text: Scriptftris, inquam, sacris incumbat christianus fidelis: ibi inueniet condigna fidei spectacula. uidebit instituentem Deum mundum suum et cum ceteris animalibus homines illam admirabilem fabricam melioremque facientem. spectabit mundum in delictis suis, iusta naufragia, piorum praemia impiorumque supplicia, maria populo siccata et de petra rursus populo maria porrecta. spectabit de caelo descendentes messes, non ex areis aratro impressas: inspiciet flumina transitus siccos refrenatis aquarum agminibus exhibentia: uidebit in quibusdam fidem cum igne luctantem, religione superatas feras et in mansuetudinem conuersas: intuebitur et animas ab ipsa iam morte reuocatas: considerabit etiam de sepulcris admirabiles ipsorum consummatorum iam uitas corporum redactas. et in his omnibus iam maius uidebit spectaculum, diabolum illum qui totum detriumphauerat mundum sub pedibus Christi iacentem. quam hoc decorum spectaculum, fratres, quam iocundum, quam necessarium? intueri semper spem suam et oculos aperire ad salutem suam. hoc est spectaculum quod uidetur etiam luminibus amissis. hoc est spectaculum quod non exhibet praetor aut consul, sed qui est solus et ante omnia et super omnia, immo ex quo omnia, pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cui laus et honor in saecula saeculorum. opto uos, fratres, bene ualere.
thought_title: The Christian's True Spectacles in Scripture
orientation: Novatian is concluding his treatise by directing the faithful Christian away from public shows and toward the spectacles found in Scripture and in God's works.
pass_a_gloss: Let the faithful Christian, I say, lean upon the sacred Scriptures: there he will find public shows worthy of [his] faith. He will see God establishing His world and, with the other animals, making human beings that admirable and better fabric. He will watch the world in its delights, just shipwrecks, the rewards of the pious and the punishments of the impious, seas dried for the people and seas again stretched out from the rock for the people. He will watch harvests descending from heaven, not pressed out from threshing floors by the plow: he will look upon rivers showing dry crossings with the ranks of waters held back: he will see in some faith wrestling with fire, wild beasts overcome by religion and turned into gentleness: he will gaze also upon souls called back from death itself: he will consider also from the tombs the admirable lives of the bodies of the perfected themselves already brought back. And in all these things he will now see a greater public show, that devil who had triumphed over the whole world lying under the feet of Christ. How fitting is this public show, brothers, how pleasant, how necessary? Always to gaze upon one's hope and to open one's eyes to one's salvation. This is the public show which is seen even with the eyes lost. This is the public show which no praetor or consul exhibits, but He who alone is both before all things and above all things, indeed from whom are all things, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and honor forever and ever. I wish you, brothers, to fare well.

lemmas.gloss: let him lean upon / devote himself to

choices.why: The verb means to lean upon or apply oneself to; 'devote himself to' captures the exhortation to sustained engagement with Scripture.
Fabrica refers to something made or constructed; 'workmanship' conveys the sense of God's creative making of human beings.
Iusta means just or righteous; the phrase refers to divinely ordained disasters upon the wicked, so 'righteous shipwrecks' preserves the moral force.
Consummatorum refers to those who have been brought to completion or perfection; 'perfected' preserves the theological sense of completed saints.
The compound verb means to triumph completely over; 'had triumphed over' keeps the pluperfect force and the military imagery.
Iocundum means delightful or pleasing; 'pleasant' is a natural English equivalent that fits the rhetorical question.

pass_b_english: Let the faithful Christian devote himself to the Scriptures, I say. There he will find public shows worthy of his faith. He will see God establishing His world, and along with the other creatures He makes human beings—that admirable workmanship, and something better still. He will watch the world in its sins: righteous shipwrecks, rewards for the godly and punishments for the ungodly, seas dried up for a people to cross, and then seas brought forth for them again from a rock (Exodus 14:21-22; Exodus 17:6). He will watch harvests come down from heaven, not pressed out of threshing floors by the plow (Exodus 16:4). He will look upon rivers that offer dry crossings while the ranks of their waters are held back (Joshua 3:17). He will see faith wrestling with fire in certain men (Daniel 3:25), wild beasts overcome by reverence and turned gentle (Daniel 6:22). He will gaze upon souls called back from death itself, and he will consider the admirable lives of the perfected, their bodies brought back from the tombs. And in all these things he will see a greater public show still: that devil who had triumphed over the whole world, now lying under the feet of Christ. How fitting is this public show, brothers—how pleasant, how necessary! To look always upon one's hope, and to open one's eyes to one's salvation. This is a public show that is seen even when one's eyes are lost. This is a public show that no praetor or consul puts on, but He who alone is before all things and above all things—indeed, from whom all things come—the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and honor forever and ever. I wish you well, brothers.

problems.quote: He will watch the world in its delights
problems.why: Latin 'delictis' means sins or crimes, not delights; the translation reverses the sense.
problems.fix: He will watch the world in its sins

edits.old: He will watch the world in its delights
edits.new: He will watch the world in its sins

fixed: Changed 'delights' to 'sins' because Latin 'delictis' means sins or crimes, not delights.

last_rejected.quote: not pressed out of threshing floors by the plow
last_rejected.why: Manna was not pressed from threshing floors; 'impressas' means imprinted/stamped by the plow, i.e., not produced by plowing.
last_rejected.fix: not imprinted on threshing floors by the plow
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'non ex areis aratro impressas' = not produced by plowing; translation conveys same meaning.

last_rejected.quote: that devil who had triumphed over the whole world
last_rejected.source_quote: diabolum illum qui totum detriumphauerat mundum
last_rejected.why: 'detriumphaverat' means had completely triumphed OVER the world, not that the devil had triumphed and the world is his; the sense is the devil who had been triumphing over the whole world.
last_rejected.fix: that devil who had been triumphing over the whole world
last_rejected.ruling: Translation matches 'who had triumphed over the whole world' as indicated by 'detriumphauerat mundum'.
